section_summary: This section consists chiefly of letters, petitions, and organizational resolutions urging the Roosevelt administration to stop or restrict American exports of arms, scrap iron, oil, gasoline, vehicles, machinery, and other war materials to Japan during its war in China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act of 1937 could embargo only enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war, would apply equally to China and Japan if invoked, and supplied no authority to prohibit exports of strategic raw materials. Correspondents therefore advocate amending the law to distinguish an aggressor from its victim, while the Department also cites its condemnation of civilian bombing and comparative arms-export license figures for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: William Hiram Foulkes urges an end to American war-supply traffic to Japan
subfiles.from: William Hiram Foulkes
subfiles.about: Foulkes asks the United States government to end trade that enables Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: Writing as a member of the Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions, Foulkes condemns Japan's aggression, the bombing of undefended cities, and the killing of Chinese noncombatants. He argues that earlier American protests are insufficient and calls for more forceful direct or indirect action against the supply traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William Hiram Foulkes on Neutrality Act limits
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why it has not invoked the Neutrality Act and what exports the law permits it to control.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a presidential finding of war would embargo enumerated arms and munitions to both China and Japan, while no statutory authority exists without such a proclamation. He stresses that the law does not cover other commodities and reports arms-export licenses of roughly $14.3 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan since July 1937.

subfiles.title: M. S. Dimmock transmits a Men's Association petition
subfiles.from: M. S. Dimmock, President, Men's Association of Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church
subfiles.to: Francis B. Sayre, Under-Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Dimmock forwards a signed statement asking the President and Congress to end American war-material traffic with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter introduces a petition adopted by members of the church's Men's Association. Dimmock also notes the congregation's pride in Sayre's work for international brotherhood.

subfiles.title: Men's Association petition against supplying Japan
subfiles.from: Members of the Men's Association of Madison Avenue Presbyterian Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: The signatories petition the federal government to halt American trade supporting Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition indicts Japan under the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and denounces attacks on Chinese civilians and foreign institutions. It cites American planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks as support for Japanese aggression and asks for every practicable means to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to M. S. Dimmock
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the Men's Association resolution and sets out the administration's legal position under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that a presidential war proclamation would stop arms shipments to both belligerents, potentially harming China as well as Japan. It adds that non-enumerated commodities cannot be prohibited and supplies comparative arms-license figures for the two countries.

subfiles.title: Lindsey Blayney protests exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Lindsey Blayney, Dean of Carleton College
subfiles.about: Blayney vehemently opposes further American exports of munitions and other commodities for Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Blayney asks the President to stop American participation in supplying Japan. He declares that he would support refusal even if it risked war with Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lindsey Blayney
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Blayney with its standard explanation of the Neutrality Act and arms-export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that the President has declined to proclaim a state of war because the Act's primary purpose is to keep the United States out of war and because an embargo would apply to both China and Japan. He notes that only formally enumerated arms and implements of war are covered and encloses the relevant resolution and pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on Derk Bodde's allegation of a Japanese loan
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes language denying departmental knowledge of any recent American loan to Japanese borrowers.
subfiles.summary: The note addresses Bodde's assertion that American bankers had recently financed Japan. It recommends stating simply that the Department knows of no recent loans obtained in the United States by Japanese borrowers.

subfiles.title: Derk Bodde denounces American economic support for Japan
subfiles.from: Derk Bodde, Lecturer in Chinese Studies, University of Pennsylvania
subfiles.about: Bodde argues that American raw materials and alleged financing make Japan's war in China possible.
subfiles.summary: Bodde describes Japan's invasion as a brutal assault on Chinese civilization and asserts that the United States supplies essential oil, scrap iron, copper, machinery dies, and other goods. He also alleges a concealed loan of about $72 million and urges Congress to end the traffic with Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Derk Bodde
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains that strategic raw materials fall outside existing embargo authority and denies knowledge of recent Japanese borrowing in the United States.
subfiles.summary: The reply outlines the Neutrality Act's equal application to both belligerents and its limitation to enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war. It states specifically that oil, scrap iron, copper, and machine dies cannot be prohibited under existing law and that the Department knows of no recent American loans to Japanese borrowers.

subfiles.title: Bent Taylor asks about sale of the Sixth Avenue Elevated as scrap
subfiles.from: Bent Taylor
subfiles.about: Taylor asks whether State Department permission is required to sell the dismantled Sixth Avenue Elevated to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief inquiry concerns a highly visible potential source of iron and steel scrap. Taylor suggests that many citizens want to know whether its purchaser may resell it to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on Sixth Avenue Elevated scrap
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost states that no existing law authorizes prohibition of iron or steel scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department interprets Taylor's inquiry as concerning scrap produced by razing the Sixth Avenue Elevated. Yost explains that the Neutrality Act is limited to arms, ammunition, and implements of war and expressly excludes iron and steel scrap.

subfiles.title: Bent Taylor thanks Charles W. Yost
subfiles.from: Bent Taylor
subfiles.about: Taylor acknowledges Yost's response to his December 6 inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Taylor briefly thanks Yost for courteously answering his question. He cites the Department's file reference for the correspondence.

subfiles.title: Richard B. Wigglesworth forwards Frank C. Seymour's letter
subfiles.from: Richard B. Wigglesworth
subfiles.about: Wigglesworth sends the State Department a constituent clergyman's appeal concerning Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The representative encloses a copy of a letter from the Reverend Frank C. Seymour of Quincy, Massachusetts. He asks for the Department's views so that he can respond to Seymour.

subfiles.title: Frank C. Seymour appeals for an end to material shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Frank C. Seymour
subfiles.about: Seymour asks Wigglesworth to stop American shipments that help Japan devastate China.
subfiles.summary: Seymour calls Japan an outrageous aggressor and contrasts American support for self-determination with exports of iron, trucks, and other materials used against China. He argues that action would command overwhelming public support and lasting gratitude.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles replies to Richard B. Wigglesworth
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles supplies material for a response to Frank C. Seymour about the Neutrality Act and exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although heavily degraded in OCR, the letter repeats the Department's explanation that a war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that existing law does not cover other commodities. It encloses the Neutrality Act resolution and International Traffic in Arms pamphlet and cites arms-license figures.

subfiles.title: Ernest H. Wilkins advocates broader action against exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Ernest H. Wilkins, President of Oberlin College
subfiles.about: Wilkins argues that the Department should discourage all munitions and war-material exports to Japan as it had discouraged aircraft exports.
subfiles.summary: Wilkins thanks Moore for an earlier letter explaining the Department's advisory action against supplying aircraft used for civilian bombing. He contends that public condemnation of broader war-material exports is equally strong and justifies comparable departmental action.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore replies to Ernest H. Wilkins
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore
subfiles.about: Moore acknowledges Wilkins's argument for broader action against exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The brief reply notes Wilkins's observations concerning munitions and war materials. Moore promises that they will receive the Department's careful consideration.

subfiles.title: T. Raymond Allston asks Hull to seek stronger neutrality legislation
subfiles.from: T. Raymond Allston
subfiles.about: Allston urges legislation permitting a selective embargo against an aggressor and covering both finished weapons and war materials.
subfiles.summary: Allston says an earlier departmental explanation showed that current law leaves Americans participating in destructive trade with Japan. He asks Hull to support broader presidential and congressional discretion so an aggressor can be identified and denied finished arms and strategic materials.

subfiles.title: Kate H. Dewing reports a San Diego protest against scrap shipments
subfiles.from: Kate H. Dewing
subfiles.about: Dewing reports a mass meeting demanding application of neutrality legislation and a ban on scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Between 500 and 600 people met near a shipment of 5,000 tons of scrap iron under the auspices of two San Diego peace groups. A motion by Lewis B. Lesley asking the President to enforce neutrality legislation and add scrap iron to the banned list passed unanimously, and Dewing says a thousand petition signatures were also sent.

subfiles.title: San Diego Peace Committee petition form
subfiles.from: San Diego Peace Committee
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: The form solicits names and addresses from persons protesting shipments of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The one-page printed form states a concise protest addressed jointly to the President and Secretary of State. It directs completed petitions to the Peace Committee on First Avenue in San Diego.

subfiles.title: J. E. Shoemaker urges amendment of the neutrality law
subfiles.from: J. E. Shoemaker
subfiles.about: Shoemaker asks Hull to hasten legislation allowing discrimination against an aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: Referring to an earlier departmental reply, Shoemaker accepts that the current neutrality law cannot stop Japan without also stopping sales to China. The difficult handwriting nevertheless clearly supports an amendment enabling the United States to single out the aggressor and correct the existing situation.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. E. Shoemaker
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges Shoemaker's proposal to amend the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes Shoemaker's further comments on conditions in East Asia. Yost assures him that his observations about amending the law will receive careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Derk Bodde renews call for an embargo and aid to China
subfiles.from: Derk Bodde
subfiles.about: Bodde argues that Japan's dependence on imported raw materials makes an embargo more important than one on finished arms and advocates an Anglo-American loan to China.
subfiles.summary: Bodde acknowledges that existing law does not permit restriction of oil, scrap iron, copper, and similar goods but insists that legislation should correct this gap. He warns that a Japanese victory would endanger the United States and England and urges American participation in contemplated British financial support for China.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Derk Bodde's follow-up
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges Bodde's proposals for embargo legislation and an American loan to China.
subfiles.summary: The reply notes Bodde's renewed observations on prohibiting vital raw-material exports to Japan. It also records his proposal for a government loan to China and promises careful consideration of both ideas.

subfiles.title: W. L. Rice endorses H.J. Res. 527 and an embargo against Japan
subfiles.from: W. L. Rice
subfiles.about: Rice supports proposed neutrality legislation intended to stop munitions and war-material exports to aggressor nations, especially Japan.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten letter is badly degraded, but it endorses a bill before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and urges the administration to support it. Rice presents refusal of war supplies to Japan as a way to restrain aggression and aid China's endangered civilians.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. L. Rice
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges Rice's endorsement of H.J. Res. 527 and explains the administration's position under the existing Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply identifies H.J. Res. 527 as Representative O'Connell's proposal to amend the Neutrality Act and promises consideration of Rice's support. It then repeats that a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to China and Japan alike, that other commodities remain outside the law, and that licensed arms exports to China exceeded those to Japan.

subfiles.title: Geneva District Conference protests exports to aggressor nations
subfiles.from: J. R. Carpenter, Secretary, Geneva District Conference
subfiles.about: Carpenter reports a unanimous Methodist conference protest against exporting any kind of war material to Japan or another aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: The resolution was adopted at Waterloo, New York, on November 18. Carpenter states that the conference represents ministers and laypeople from sixty-five churches with a combined membership of 13,000.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to J. R. Carpenter
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the Methodist conference protest and explains the legal limits of export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Carpenter for communicating the conference's unanimous views. It explains the equal application of any Neutrality Act embargo to China and Japan, the exclusion of non-enumerated commodities, and comparative arms-export license totals.

subfiles.title: San Pedro Writers' Guild protests strategic exports to Japan
subfiles.from: R. Louise Emery, Secretary, San Pedro Writers' Guild
subfiles.about: Emery asks the President to stop shipments of scrap iron, oil, and other war necessities to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Emery argues that American supplies enable the killing of Chinese civilians and warns that Japanese expansion, backed by Germany and Italy, may eventually threaten the United States and the Pacific. She describes strong opposition among San Pedro longshoremen and civic groups, while noting that labor contracts compel longshoremen to load cargo supplied by shipowners.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to R. Louise Emery
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains why existing law cannot stop exports of scrap iron, oil, and similar commodities to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeats that invoking the Neutrality Act would prohibit enumerated arms to both China and Japan. It specifically notes that scrap iron, oil, and similar products are outside the statutory list and concludes with comparative arms-license figures.

subfiles.title: Rauschenbusch Social Problems Club letter advocating a comprehensive embargo
subfiles.from: Members of the Rauschenbusch Social Problems Club
subfiles.about: Student ministers call for complete American economic withdrawal from Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The writers praise administration peace efforts but argue that the United States supplies more than half of Japan's imported war materials. They advocate an embargo on gasoline, oil, scrap and other metals, vehicles, machinery, munitions, and convertible goods, contending that moral integrity and continued friendship with an independent China outweigh temporary economic losses.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to the Rauschenbusch Social Problems Club
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost explains that gasoline, oil, automobiles, and other requested embargo items are not covered by the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply lays out the consequences of a proclamation applying equally to China and Japan and the limited statutory definition of arms and implements of war. It expressly states that gasoline, oil, automobiles, and similar products cannot be prohibited and supplies export-license totals.

subfiles.title: St. John's congregational petition against trade supporting Japan
subfiles.from: Members of P. Nelson Schlegel's congregation
subfiles.about: Congregants ask the President to end American trade that supports Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition repeats charges that Japan violated the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and that American planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks facilitate aggression. Its two pages carry numerous handwritten signatures from members of the congregation.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to P. Nelson Schlegel
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges Schlegel's congregational petition and explains export-law limits and the Department's position on civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that a Neutrality Act proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that scrap iron, oil, and similar products cannot be barred under existing law. It also says the government has repeatedly condemned civilian bombing and has communicated that condemnation to American aircraft and aeronautical-equipment manufacturers and exporters.

subfiles.title: Clarence C. Beasley transmits a Friends of China resolution
subfiles.from: Clarence C. Beasley, President, Friends of China, Inc.
subfiles.about: Beasley sends a unanimously adopted resolution seeking a more positive United States policy in East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Beasley says the resolution expresses only the minimum convictions of the Friends of China. He emphasizes that the society's members know China and East Asian affairs and that their position reflects both informed judgment and broader American sympathies.

subfiles.title: Friends of China resolution against American support for Japan
subfiles.from: Friends of China, Inc.
subfiles.about: The resolution asks the President to end American trade that assists Japan's aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The organization condemns Japan's violations of the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact, attacks on civilians, and destruction in China. It identifies American raw materials, aircraft, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks as enabling the war and calls for every practicable direct or indirect remedy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Clarence C. Beasley
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost responds to the Friends of China resolution with the Department's legal and policy position.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that an arms embargo under the Neutrality Act would apply to both sides and that scrap iron, oil, and similar products cannot be restricted under existing legislation. It also cites the government's public condemnation of civilian bombing and its warning to American aircraft manufacturers and exporters.

subfiles.title: Greenville College Student Association transmits its resolution
subfiles.from: Student Association of Greenville College
subfiles.about: The student association forwards a deliberated resolution concerning American participation in the Sino-Japanese War.
subfiles.summary: The writers emphasize that the resolution followed a cool presentation of facts rather than emotional oratory and that action was delayed for a week to permit reflection. They report overwhelming approval and ask Hull to help end the conflict and American participation in it.

subfiles.title: Greenville College resolution to limit war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Student Association and faculty of Greenville College
subfiles.to: United States government officials and the press
subfiles.about: The resolution urges restrictions on a broad range of American war materials exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The students and faculty identify Japan as an aggressor and deplore American profits from Chinese suffering. They call for exports of munitions, oil, gasoline, chemicals, iron, aircraft, automobiles, and associated parts to be halted or reduced to peacetime levels and encourage other colleges to protest.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Greenville College Student Association
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the Greenville College resolution and repeats the Department's interpretation of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply says a presidential proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan and that the President has declined to act after considering the statute's peacekeeping purpose and surrounding circumstances. It adds that the Act cannot reach commodities outside its arms list and provides comparative license values.

subfiles.title: Clayton S. Valder forwards a North Omaha petition
subfiles.from: Clayton S. Valder
subfiles.about: Valder sends a petition unanimously approved by 125 men from six North Omaha churches.
subfiles.summary: The group met at Miller Park Presbyterian Church on November 28. Acting as chairman, Valder forwards the resolution to the President on their behalf.

subfiles.title: North Omaha churchmen's petition against supplying Japan
subfiles.from: One hundred twenty-five men representing six North Omaha churches
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: The petition asks the federal government to end American trade contributing to the destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese aggression, civilian bombing, and the destruction of schools, churches, hospitals, and businesses. It identifies American raw materials, planes, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks as supporting Japan and invokes the Good Neighbor principle in requesting action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Clayton S. Valder
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the North Omaha petition and explains the Department's legal limits and policy against civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Valder for transmitting the resolution and promises appropriate attention. It outlines the Neutrality Act's equal effect on China and Japan, cites arms-license values, and notes official condemnation of civilian bombing and material encouragement through aircraft supplies.

subfiles.title: T. Raymond Allston asks Roosevelt for selective embargo authority
subfiles.from: T. Raymond Allston
subfiles.about: Allston urges the President to seek legislation permitting embargoes against an aggressor without denying the victim means of self-defense.
subfiles.summary: Allston recounts his earlier correspondence with Cordell Hull and concludes that current law forces the United States into indirect participation in Japan's war. He calls for discretionary authority to identify an aggressor and prohibit both finished implements of war and strategic materials, linking this proposal to Roosevelt's quarantine concept.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to T. Raymond Allston
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges both of Allston's December 7 letters advocating amendment of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The response covers Allston's letter to the State Department and the parallel letter referred by the White House. Yost states that his observations on amendment of the Act have been noted and will receive careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Evanston correspondent forwards letters to Illinois senators
subfiles.from: Unidentified correspondent, 625 Emerson Street, Evanston
subfiles.about: An Evanston correspondent sends Hull copies of letters urging Illinois senators to revise neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: The writer says Walter Judd spoke favorably of Hull's position on neutrality before an Evanston audience of more than 300 women and 450 men. The enclosed letters express the writer's views and, in the writer's judgment, those of the audience.

subfiles.title: Letter to Senator Scott Lucas advocating neutrality-law revision
subfiles.from: Unidentified correspondent, 625 Emerson Street, Evanston
subfiles.about: The writer asks Lucas to amend neutrality law so that the United States does not assist an aggressor.
subfiles.summary: Citing Walter Judd, the writer alleges that American scrap iron, high-test gasoline, trucks, and cars sustain Japan's army and place Chinese foot soldiers at a severe disadvantage. The letter warns that a Japanese victory could eventually threaten the United States and criticizes cash-and-carry language for treating aggressor and victim alike.

subfiles.title: Letter to Senator James Hamilton Lewis advocating neutrality-law revision
subfiles.from: Unidentified correspondent, 625 Emerson Street, Evanston
subfiles.about: The writer asks Lewis to revise neutrality law so American supplies no longer assist an aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: This companion letter repeats the argument that American scrap iron, gasoline, vehicles, and other goods keep Japan's army in the field. It invokes Walter Judd's observations from China, warns of a future Japanese threat, and objects that cash-and-carry rules put an aggressor and its victim on the same footing.
